title: How to Use a Mandoline to Make Uniform Parsnip Crisps
meta_description: Master the art of homemade parsnip crisps with a mandoline. Learn how to get restaurant-thin, uniform slices for the perfect crunch every time.
html:
There is something deeply satisfying about a root vegetable chip that actually crunches. When you try to slice parsnips with a chef's knife, you often end up with a mix of thick chunks and paper-thin shards. The result? Half your batch is burnt while the other half is soggy.

The secret to professional-grade homemade parsnip crisps mandoline style is consistency. When every slice is the exact same thickness, they cook at the same rate, giving you that gold-standard snap. Using a high-quality Mandoline Slicer allows you to achieve those restaurant-thin slices quickly and safely, taking the guesswork out of the prep work.

Choosing and Prepping Your Parsnips

Before you even touch your slicer, start with the right produce. Look for parsnips that are straight and firm. Avoid the ones with deep curves or knots, as these are harder to glide across a blade and can lead to uneven pieces.

Scrub your parsnips thoroughly under cold water to remove any lingering soil. You don't necessarily need to peel them—the skin is edible and adds a rustic look—but if you prefer a cleaner, more refined crisp, use a vegetable peeler first. Trim off the woody top and the very tip of the root to create a stable cylinder for slicing.

Setting Up Your Mandoline Slicer for Maximum Crunch

To get that perfect crisp, you want a slice that is roughly 1/16th of an inch. If the slice is too thick, the parsnip will stay chewy in the center; too thin, and they will vanish into smoke the moment they hit the oil.

This is where the Mandoline Slicer shines. Because it features adjustable settings, you can dial in the exact thickness you need. Once you've set your blade, always use the included hand guard. Parsnips can be slippery, and the blades on a professional slicer are incredibly sharp. The guard keeps your fingertips far away from the edge while ensuring you get every last slice out of the root.

Step-by-Step Guide to Homemade Parsnip Crisps Mandoline Style

Consistency is key, but the process after slicing is what determines the final texture. Follow these steps for the best results:

  • Slice: Glide the parsnip across the Mandoline Slicer in a steady, fluid motion. Collect your slices in a large bowl.
  • Rinse: Parsnips are high in starch. Rinse the slices in cold water until the water runs clear. This prevents them from sticking together in the pan.
  • Dry: This is the most skipped but most important step. Pat the slices completely dry with a clean kitchen towel or paper towels. Water in the oil causes splattering and prevents crisping.
  • Season: Toss the dry slices in a bowl with a small amount of neutral oil (like grapeseed or canola) and a pinch of salt.
  • Fry or Bake: For frying, heat oil to 325°F and fry in small batches. For baking, spread them in a single layer on a parchment-lined sheet at 375°F for about 15-20 minutes, flipping halfway through.

Avoiding Common Pitfalls

The most common mistake when making homemade parsnip crisps is overcrowding the pan. If you dump too many slices into the oil at once, the temperature drops, and the parsnips will absorb the oil instead of searing. Work in batches, leaving plenty of room for the slices to float freely.

Another tip is to keep a close eye on the color. Parsnips have a higher sugar content than potatoes, meaning they can go from golden brown to burnt in a matter of seconds. Remove them from the heat just as they begin to turn golden; they will continue to crisp up as they cool on a wire rack.

Cleaning and Maintaining Your Gear

Since parsnips are starchy, they can leave a residue on your slicing surface. To keep your Mandoline Slicer performing at its peak, rinse it immediately after use with warm, soapy water. Avoid using abrasive scrubbing pads on the blades, as you want to maintain that razor-sharp edge for your next batch of veggie chips.

If your mandoline has an adjustable dial, make sure it's clicked firmly into place before you start. A shifting blade mid-slice is a recipe for uneven chips and potential safety hazards.

FAQ

Can I use a mandoline for other root vegetable crisps?

Absolutely. The same technique works perfectly for carrots, beets, and sweet potatoes. Just remember to adjust your thickness based on the density of the vegetable; beets often require a slightly thicker slice than parsnips.

Why are my parsnip chips curling in the oven?

Curling is natural, but if they are curling too much, it's usually because they aren't weighted down or spaced out. Using a silicone baking mat or rotating the pan frequently can help maintain a flatter shape.

How do I store these once they are cooled?

Store your crisps in an airtight container or a heavy-duty zip-top bag. If they lose their crunch after a day or two, you can pop them in a 300°F oven for 3-5 minutes to refresh them.
